title: The Tilt That Makes the Seasons
blurb: Earth leans over as it circles the sun, and that small lean gives us spring, summer, fall, and winter.

1.title: The Tilt That Makes the Seasons
1.subtitle: A read-together story for ages 3 to 4
1.intro: Read this story out loud together. Point to the picture as you go.

meta.templateLabel: The Tilt That Makes the Seasons

blocks.prompt: Look at the picture. Find the tree in each season.

notes: There are four seasons
Leaves grow in spring
Leaves fall in fall
Snow can come in winter
The sun feels warm in summer

blocks.prompt: Read this out loud
blocks.text: The year goes around and around. In spring, tiny green leaves pop out. In summer, the days are long and warm. In fall, the leaves turn yellow and red. Then they let go and drift down. In winter, the tree is bare and the air is cold. Then spring comes back and the leaves grow again. The tree does this every year.

blocks.prompt: Why the Year Changes
blocks.text: Earth spins like a top, but it does not spin straight up. It leans a little to one side. Earth also travels all the way around the sun, and that trip takes one whole year. Because of the lean, your part of Earth tips toward the sun for part of the year. Then the days are long and the sun feels strong. That is summer. Later in the trip, your part tips away. The days get short and the sun feels weak. That is winter. Spring and fall are the in between times. The lean never changes. Only your side of the trip does.

3.title: The Tilt That Makes the Seasons
3.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 7 to 8
3.intro: Read the passage, then work through each part. You can look back at the passage any time.

meta.templateLabel: The Tilt That Makes the Seasons

blocks.prompt: It Is Not About Getting Closer
blocks.text: Many people think summer happens because Earth moves closer to the sun. That is not the reason. Here is a surprise: Earth is at its closest to the sun in early January, right in the middle of a northern winter. The real reason is the tilt. Earth spins on an imaginary line called its axis, and that axis is tipped over by about 23 degrees. The tilt always points the same direction, like a leaning pole that never straightens. As Earth travels around the sun, the northern half spends part of the year leaning toward the sun. During those months the sun climbs higher in the sky, its light hits the ground more directly, and the days stretch out longer. That is summer. Six months later the northern half leans away. The sun stays low, its light spreads out thin across the ground, and the days shrink. That is winter. This also means the two halves of Earth never agree. When it is July and hot in Canada, it is July and cold in Argentina.

4.title: The Tilt That Makes the Seasons

meta.templateLabel: The Tilt That Makes the Seasons

blocks.prompt: The Angle of the Light
blocks.text: The seasons are not caused by distance. They are caused by angle. Earth's axis, the imaginary line it spins around, is tilted about 23.4 degrees, and that tilt stays pointed in the same direction all year while the planet loops around the sun. So for half the orbit the northern half of Earth leans sunward, and for the other half it leans away. Leaning toward the sun does two things at once. The sun rises higher in the sky, so its light strikes the ground steeply and delivers more energy to each patch of soil. It also stays up longer, so the ground has more hours to soak that energy up. Shine a flashlight straight down on a table and you get a small bright circle. Tip the flashlight and the same light smears into a large dim oval. Winter is the tipped flashlight. Four days mark the corners of the year. The two solstices are the longest and shortest days, when the tilt is aimed most directly toward or away from the sun. The two equinoxes fall halfway between, when neither half leans and daylight and darkness are close to equal everywhere. Not every place gets four seasons. Near the equator the sun stays high all year, so the calendar is split into wet and dry seasons instead, ruled by rain rather than temperature. Near the poles the tilt is so extreme that the sun refuses to set for weeks in summer and never rises for weeks in winter.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Axial tilt: 23.4 degrees, held steady by the moon

blocks.prompt: A Lean of Twenty Three Degrees
blocks.text: Earth's orbit is very close to a circle, and the small stretch it does have works against the popular story. The planet reaches perihelion, its closest approach to the sun, in the first days of January, while the northern half of the world is deep in winter. Distance is not what builds a season. Geometry is. Earth's rotational axis leans 23.4 degrees away from vertical, and gyroscopic stability keeps that lean pointed at roughly the same distant patch of sky all year long. As the planet moves through its orbit, then, one hemisphere is presented to the sun and the other is turned aside. Being presented to the sun changes two things. First, insolation, the amount of solar energy landing on each square meter of ground, rises sharply because the light arrives steeply rather than at a glancing angle. Second, daylight lengthens, giving the surface more hours to absorb that energy than it has to radiate it back at night. Heat accumulates. Six months later the arrangement reverses, radiation outpaces absorption, and heat drains away. That balance explains a detail people often find strange. The longest day of the year is not the hottest day of the year. Land and ocean take weeks to catch up to the change in energy, so the warmest stretch usually lands a month or more after the solstice. Scientists call this seasonal lag, and it is the same reason the coldest weeks arrive well after the shortest day. Living things read the season by light rather than warmth, which is more reliable. As nights lengthen, a deciduous tree pulls valuable nitrogen and other nutrients back out of its leaves and shuts down chlorophyll production. The green fades, and the yellow and orange pigments that were present in the leaf all summer are finally revealed. The tree is not putting on a show. It is closing accounts before the cold arrives.

6.title: The Tilt That Makes the Seasons
6.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for age 13
6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

meta.templateLabel: The Tilt That Makes the Seasons

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Obliquity: Earth's 23.4 degree axial tilt
The moon keeps that tilt from wandering wildly
Perihelion in January, aphelion in July
Milankovitch cycles shift tilt and orbit over tens of thousands of years
Photoperiod, not temperature, triggers most plant and animal timing
Uranus is tilted about 98 degrees and rolls on its side

blocks.prompt: Twenty Three Degrees: The Small Lean That Runs the Year
blocks.text: Almost everything you associate with a season traces back to a single number: 23.4 degrees. That is Earth's obliquity, the angle between its rotational axis and a line drawn perpendicular to its orbital plane. Because a spinning body resists changes to its orientation, the axis holds that lean steady, aimed at nearly the same point in the sky for the whole journey around the sun. The planet does not nod toward the sun and away again. It keeps a fixed posture while its position changes, and that is enough. The consequence is that each hemisphere alternates between being presented to the sunlight and being turned aside from it. Two effects follow, and they reinforce each other. Sunlight arriving steeply concentrates its energy onto a small area, while the same beam arriving at a glancing angle smears across a much larger one. At the same time, the presented hemisphere receives more hours of daylight, so absorption gets a longer run than nighttime radiation does. Energy accumulates through late spring and early summer, then drains through fall. This accumulation model explains something that a simpler distance model cannot. The hottest weeks of the year do not coincide with the longest day. Oceans and soil have enormous thermal mass and respond slowly, so peak temperatures typically arrive four to eight weeks after the summer solstice, and the coldest weeks arrive well after the shortest day. Meteorologists call this seasonal lag, and coastal regions, backed by even slower water, lag longer than the interiors of continents. The distance story fails a second test as well. Earth reaches perihelion, its closest point to the sun, in early January, and aphelion, its farthest, in early July. If proximity governed seasons, January would be the warm month everywhere on Earth, and it plainly is not. What proximity actually does is subtle: it makes southern summers marginally more intense and southern winters marginally milder than their northern counterparts, an effect the vast southern oceans largely absorb. Life on the surface has evolved to read this cycle, and it mostly reads it through light rather than heat. Photoperiod, the length of the day, repeats with mechanical precision each year, while temperature is erratic and can lie. A warm week in February proves nothing. So a deciduous tree responds to lengthening nights by withdrawing nitrogen and phosphorus from its leaves, dismantling its chlorophyll, and revealing the carotenoid pigments that were sitting in the leaf all summer, masked by green. The tree is not decorating the season. It is salvaging the expensive parts of an organ it is about to discard. Even the tilt itself is not permanent. Over cycles measured in tens of thousands of years, Earth's obliquity drifts between roughly 22.1 and 24.5 degrees, and the shape and orientation of its orbit shift alongside it. These slow variations, known as Milankovitch cycles, alter how sunlight is distributed across latitudes and seasons, and they help pace the advance and retreat of ice ages. Our moon is part of why the drift stays small. Its gravitational steadying keeps Earth's axis from wandering the way an unpartnered planet's can. Seen that way, a calm October afternoon is the visible end of a very long chain: a moon holding an axis, an axis holding an angle, and an angle deciding how a beam of light meets the ground.
